rule: a relative import out of a pack
why:
`packs/`, THE THIRD WORKSPACE ROOT, ONE FIXTURE PER TEXT GATE THAT READS IT. Each tree holds a violation under `packs/` and nothing a gate reading only `packages` and `apps` could find, so dropping `packs` from a gate's list turns its case red here. That is the defect an audit found: all four text gates had the pair written in, and read green over four shipped packs they had never opened. `tools/gates/test/packs-read.test.mjs` proves the same four under `node --test`; this is the copy `run.mjs` runs, so it cannot be skipped by a run that does not reach the unit tests. Measured on 24 September by deleting `packs` from each gate's list in a scratch copy: `em-dash-packs` went red with exit 3 (nothing read), `secret-grep-packs` and `graph-packs` each passed their seeded violation.

THE DECOYS ARE THE PACK'S TEST, which sits beside the file it ships rather than under `test/`. `em-dash` and `graph` must leave it alone and it carries the same sentence and the same climb as the seeded file, so `packs/seeded/` named twice is the gate reading the test. `secret-grep` reads tests on purpose, so its decoy is a line logging the key's label beside the one logging its value.

NO `shell-words-packs`, AND THAT IS THE GATE'S DECISION RATHER THAN A GAP. Its words are the use cases the core must not name, and a pack is where a use case belongs, so it leaves `packs` out on purpose (its `WORKSPACES` header) and `packs-read.test.mjs` pins the pair: a use-case word in a pack stays green, the same word in `packages/kernel` goes red. A negative here would be a fixture asserting the opposite of the rule.
